Now, the hymn of praise.
[She who has] the form of an unbroken circle; [she who is] the three threads; [she who is] Mahāmāyā; [she who is] the three gods; [she who is] Piṅgākṣī; [she who is] Kṣetrayā;
[she who is] Raktāmbarajvalinī; [she who is] Vaṭukayā; [she who is] Hantārṣārkhodaduḥkhasā; [she who is] Gaṇayā.
The syllable *ū* and so forth: Brahmāyaṇī; standing in the middle; having six pillars; dark blue and red.
Utphullā, Sāṃtakāgni, and Aindrī.
The horn-tip.
In her childhood state she is Mahāraudrī, and as a maiden she is Raktarocanī;
she wears a red garment and her body is crimson with vermilion.
Four-armed, holding a spear, a trident, and the auspicious vessel of accomplishment (siddhipātra),
she is the supreme youthful power (kaumāra-śakti) borne upon a magnificent peacock.
The goddess Raktādevī, clad in red garments and possessing a red complexion,
is to be worshipped with *kola* fruits in the great field (*mahākṣetra*) where she dwells in the banyan tree.
O Kaumārī, who dwells eternally on the southern seat, salutations to you!
With an upright staff, the crusher of the heads of the gods, worshipped by Kādyāri,
the supreme bearer of Brahmā’s severed head, holding a *ḍamaru* drum and a *khaṭvāṅga* staff,
he is the Lord who is to be honored at the feet by Brahmāṇī and the excellent group of Mothers.
The Lord Mahābhairava reigns within the hollow of the mountain.
I bow to Nāṭeśvara, who is adorned with the power of bliss, whose essence is mantra, who accords with reality, who is the cause for all purposes without exception,
who effects the eightfold accomplishment, who is the supreme form, and who grants all siddhis.
By Nāṭeśvarī.
O Goddess, dweller in the center of the sacred seat (pīṭha), seated upon a corpse, beautiful, with a red body, who wields a trident and a sword, the bestower of the essence of cyclic existence,
you who are always worshipped by Brahmā, Upendra, Surendra, Kinnaras, and men.
I constantly bow my head to the Goddess, who bestows the accomplishment of all desires and purposes.
Surrounded by Brahmāṇī and the others, such as Jayā, she stands in the sacred field; Amṛtā resides on the bank of the Śrītīra river, while Sakuleśvarī holds a trident and a rosary.
Unmattā wields a discus and a conch, and Pīyūṣā holds a mace.
May the Mistress of the Wheel (Cakreśvarī), together with the bindu of Mālāvarakā and the others, protect [me].
May Cakreśvarī— red in color, four-armed, and holding a rosary, a trident, a skull-cup, and a hand-disk— protect you!
Homage to you, Cakreśvarī, who is red in color, has four arms, and holds a rosary, a trident, a water-pot, and a dot in her hands.
With a small amount of mercury.

Āṃ kroṃ aiṃ hrīṃ! O Kumārī, proclaim, proclaim! O you whose passion is the *kimakhirekekiyā*, perform the mudrās, numbers, and so forth in the wheel! (2) To the one who acts once for the sake of the illustrious Guhyacaṇḍa, the Lord of Siddhis known as Tejas, the supreme among the excellent mind and wind, the intense one who holds the command!
May there be solitude in the middle of the night; homage to you, the one who has gone to the treasure and the creator of existence.
Seated upon the throne of the syllable Aiṃ, standing atop a vajra and lotus,
I bow to the Goddess Śrī Kubjikā, who has transcended the sixfold time.
Smoky in appearance, with matted locks possessing the luster of molten gold, adorned with three eyes and a tilaka;

holding in his hands a sword and a flaying knife, as well as a sharp trident, a skull-cup, and at the end of a wheel, various kinds of human flesh and blood, he stands upon a corpse in the form of a *preta*.
I bow to Ucchiṣṭanātha, together with Mātaṅgī and Śrī, surrounded by his own retinue.
She is Vaiṣṇavī, the illusion of Viṣṇu, the destroyer of the formidable fortresses of the Daityas;
her body is greenish-yellow in hue, and she is seated upon Garuḍa.
Holding a conch, a discus, and a mace in her hands, she is adorned with four arms;
she is the great play of blazing jewels, embellished with various gems.
Always bearing the *haripuṣpa* flower and fragrance, she remains in the form of a green creeper, established in heaven, on earth, and in the netherworld (*pātāla*).
O Nārāyaṇī, who dwells in the kadamba tree in the great field of Aṭṭahāsa and resides upon the seat in the southwest— salutations to you!
In the east, south, west, north, and northeast, [one should worship] Śivā; in the east and other directions, Vāmāśikā, Kṣetreśa, Vahni (Agni), Tapanāniraya (Sūrya), Heramba (Gaṇeśa), and Nātha;
and in the cremation ground, the omnipresent Ādideva with four arms, who bestows the fruit of all desires.
The valid cognition consisting of eternal bliss is always strengthened by offerings, worship, and other such practices.
"According to the vehicle, according to the exertion," and so forth. [This is] the statement.
Thus ends the Night Offering (niśibalyārccana).
Then, having gone to the bathing pavilion in the northeast corner and having placed the deity there— whether it be made of heartwood,
or silver, or copper, or stone, or wood, or clay— the image of the deity is installed.
Having placed [the deity] in the center of an eight-petaled lotus within the outer mandala, one should draw four triangles on the outside.
With yellow powder, [one should draw] the divine auspicious throne-seat (devabhadrapīṭhāsana) and a mirror; at the four corners, the oceans.
The first worship: Homage to the Salt Ocean; homage to the Naga King Ananta.
Worship at the eastern face; thus [ends] the east.
To the Southern Ocean, *namaḥ*. To the Naga Takṣaka, *namaḥ*.
Worship with the southern face, worship with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and the Gāyatrī mantra. Thus ends the Southern Ocean.

In the west: *Namaḥ* to Surodasamudra; *namaḥ* to Padmanāga. Worship with the western face. Worship with the armor-mantra (*kavaca*) beginning with *padma*. Worship with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and the *Gāyatrī*. Thus ends the western ocean.
Utthala Ocean. Homage to the Ikṣu Ocean. Homage to the Saṅkhapāla Nāga.
Worship with the northern face; worship with the mantra of the eye, *okhadhī*.
First, by means of the root-mantra: ashes, water from the Gaṅgā, fruit-water, and water from the Bhīṣma-tīrtha.
Worship with the root mantra; worship with the three powders using the weapon mantra. Thus ends the northern ocean.

Then follows the etymological derivation (*nirvacana*) and so forth; the protection against fire and iron; then the bathing of the deity. One should recite [the following] starting from today: first, the ocean bath with one's respective mantra; then the clay bath for the heart with the *hṛdaya* mantra; and the bath with earth for the head with the *śiras* mantra.

With the *pallava* (sprout) and *śikhā* mantras; with the *pañcāmṛta-gāyatrī*; with the armor (*kavaca*) of Padmā and others; with the *pañcagavya-gāyatrī*; with the eye (*netra*) of Oṃ-kha-dhī; with the weapon (*astra*) of the three powders—barley, wheat, and *bilva*; with all the waters using the root mantra; with the ashes using the root mantra; with the root mantra in seven streams or a thousand streams; [and] with the root mantra.
A sacrificial session or a thousand [offerings], a ritual bath in water according to one's capacity, and a gift of grain as alms.
The sprinkling with seeds, the sprinkling with clay, the sprinkling with fruits, and the sprinkling with water—these [are performed] with the root mantra.
Thus is the bath.
Then follows the dressing in garments, the application of collyrium, sandalwood paste, vermilion, and the inspection of the lamp.
Garland of flowers | fruit |
With attributes; incense; lamp; benediction; various ornaments and so forth.

Having circumambulated the Devavagarambā Maṇḍapa and performed the *jātrā* ceremony, one should then cause her to enter through the southwest gate by the hand of a young woman. [This includes] the ritual of sprinkling water (*nirvvacchanādi*), the protection against fire (*agnirakṣādi*), the protection against iron (*loharakṣā*), and the possession of virtuous qualities (*saguṇa*).
The sacrificer should perform the scattering of parched grains (*lājākṣepaṇa*), cause [the bride] to enter the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), and recite the *svastivācana*.
Having stood upon a svastika to the east of the fire-pit.
In the center, there is a triangle, a hexagon, a circle of fire, and a lotus with twelve petals joined with eight petals;
on the ground, one should place the syllable *laṃ* together with a water-pot (*kalaśa*) upon that path, which grants all desired objects.
This is the excellent wheel. Adorned with four gates, it is peerless; outside that, there is one auspicious square.
Therein, the host of world-protectors beginning with Indra and Agni should be worshipped from the east onwards, bestowing happiness.
The Kṣatrapāla should be worshipped; furthermore, in the center, the deity Siddhilakṣmī is to be worshipped with effort by practitioners for the sake of accomplishment. (***) (FīṅūṛE)
[Blank folio] Descended from heaven during the day, you have protected that circle of men by assuming a human body.

"In accordance with my capacity and as is fitting for the sacrifice performed by me,
this vessel belonging to Indra is especially your portion."
O Lord of the Earth, let this mental joy be grasped by your mind;
O Master, may all that was devoid of honor be forgiven.
From today onwards.

I, Śrī Sumatijayajitāmitramalla, for the sake of pleasing my chosen deity, have performed the consecration of the temple of Śrī Nṛtyeśvara Lakṣmīdevī, the hoisting of the golden pinnacle and banner upon it, and the great sacrificial festival of ten million oblations of perfected fire, including the narrative of the slaying of Yama. Śrī...
For the purpose of performing the five-fold ritual service (*pañcopacāra-pūjā*) to Nṛtyeśvara, this statement was made during the sacrifice of ten million oblations (*koṭyāhuti-yajña*).

The lunar day (tithi) increased by the weekday and divided by forty; if the remainder is zero, there is fire on earth; for the sake of happiness in a fire-oblation, if the remainder is two, there is loss of life and wealth in heaven and on earth.
Tell me, by what remainder is the sum of the lunar day and the weekday plus one divided by fire (three) and space (zero)—
that which destroys wealth and life?
In Pātāla, with two remaining, there is the destruction of accumulated wealth;
on Earth, with four remaining, it bestows abundant happiness.
The illustrious holder of the [initiation] lineage has come to the king for the sake of Indrakalaśa.
O Blessed One, Lord of the World of Men, King of Men, Sovereign of Men,
you are manifestly the Thousand-Eyed One, the Three... [eyes].

(BḷāṇK) Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa. The Bhairava Pūjā. Beginning with the salutation to the Guru. The water-vessel, the *argha*-vessel, and self-worship. The invocation of Śrī Saṃvartā. The Three Deities. Dharma and so forth.
The foundational power (ādhāra-śakti) and so forth. Homage to the solar disc (sūrya-maṇḍala). Homage to the lunar disc (soma-maṇḍala).
Homage to the circle of fire (agnimaṇḍala). [Offer] the preta-seat and the lion-seat. [Perform] the triple añjali.
Meditative absorption.
The face of Īśāna, however, is upward-facing; it is the form of emanation, both supreme and non-supreme, resembling snow, the kunda flower, and the moon, and like pure crystal.
He causes the entire world to expand by means of the rays of the moon's beams,
raining down a great flood of streams resembling nectar.
Thus, salutation to the flower of meditative absorption. [With] three añjalis.

Homage to Bhairava. Hrāṃ, homage to Vidyārāja Bhairava. [Salutations] to Indra and the others.
The six-limbed mantra of the face.
Bali.
Oṃ kṣetropakṣetra saṃdoha oṃ hūṃ haḥ! To all the field-protectors (*kṣetrapāla*), accept this offering of perfume, incense, and bali.
(2) Homage, homage! [This is] the root mantra. [Perform] the triple añjali, the *śakti* mudrā, and offer incense and lamps.

Recitation: Praise: "Akhaṇḍamaṇḍala," and so forth. We praise Svacchanda Bhairava, whose form is supreme light, the sole uniform nature of the universe, the soul of the universe, and the singular cause of everything in the universe.
Salutations to the ocean Bhairava, the repository of all prosperity, whose playful surging waves are the spreading powers of his energy.
